---
title: "The Reading Gap? How schools in Ontario Compare"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# install packages if they are missing
pkgs <- c("tidyverse", "scales")
new_pkgs <- pkgs[!(pkgs %in% installed.packages()[, "Package"])]
if (length(new_pkgs) > 0) install.packages(new_pkgs, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
library(tidyverse)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
source("A2-data-cleaning.R")
```

```{r style, include = FALSE}
# Colours: income fifths (blue = affluent, rust = high-poverty)
income_cols <- c("Most affluent fifth"   = "#2E6F9E",
                 "Second fifth"          = "#7FA7C6",
                 "Middle fifth"          = "#ADADAD",
                 "Fourth fifth"          = "#D9886F",
                 "Highest-poverty fifth" = "#B5432A")

# Colours: share of students whose first language is not English (light to dark)
lang_cols <- c("10% or fewer"  = "#CFC3E6",
               "10% to 30%"    = "#9479C4",
               "More than 30%" = "#4B2C8A")

source_note <- paste("Source: Ontario Ministry of Education school information",
                     "(STA313 datasets). Averages of English-language public",
                     "and Catholic elementary schools.")

# 2017 -> "2017-18"
year_label <- function(y) paste0(y, "-", substr(y + 1, 3, 4))

# One theme for every chart
theme_story <- theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12.5),
        plot.title.position = "plot",
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey30"),
        plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey45", size = 7.5, hjust = 0),
        plot.caption.position = "plot",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "top",
        legend.justification = "left")
```


Reading is a fundamental skill that shapes how students learn, communicate, and navigate everyday life. It is the foundation for learning across different subjects, from solving mathematical word problems, to understanding science and history. Students who developed a solid foundation in reading by Grade 3 are more likely to succeed academically, while those who struggle at an early stage may face challenges in their later education if these difficulties are not addressed. 

Since 2017, students in Ontario have experienced significant disruptions to their education, including school closures due to pandemic, two years of cancelled assessments, and ongoing debates over how reading should be taught. Nevertheless, the overall reading performance appears remarkably stable. In 2017-18, about 74% of Grade 3 students across Ontario met the provincial reading standard. By 2024-25, the figure remained approximately the same.

However, overall provincial figures may overlook significant variations in reading performance across schools. Using school-level reading results across Ontario, this article explores the relationship between students’ socioeconomic backgrounds and student reading achievement. How large is the performance gap between the most affluent and high-poverty schools, and has it narrowed over time? Do high-poverty schools make greater progress by Grade 6? Additionally, does the proportion of students whose first language is not English relate to reading performance?


## Has provincial reading changed since 2017?

```{r s1-data}
avg_year <- elem |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(`Grade 3` = mean(g3_read, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Grade 6` = mean(g6_read, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Grade 3`, `Grade 6`), names_to = "grade", values_to = "pct") |>

  mutate(period = if_else(year < "2020", "before", "after"),
         year_short = year_label(as.integer(substr(year, 1, 4))))
```

```{r fig1, fig.height = 3.8}
ggplot(avg_year, aes(x = year_short, y = pct, colour = grade,
                     group = paste(grade, period))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +

  geom_vline(xintercept = 2.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  annotate("text", x = 2.5, y = 64, label = "no tests in\n2019-20 and 2020-21",
           size = 3, colour = "grey40") +

  geom_text(data = filter(avg_year, year == "2024-2025"),
            aes(label = paste0(grade, ": ", round(pct), "%")),
            hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.1, size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Grade 3" = "#333333", "Grade 6" = "#8C8C8C"),
                      guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.4, 1.3))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(60, 92), labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Figure 1. The provincial average barely moves",
       subtitle = "Average share of students meeting the provincial reading standard",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = source_note) +
  theme_story
```

Overall, the provincial average shows that in the average school around 74% of Grade 3 students met the standard in both 2017-18 and 2024-25 (Figure 1). There was a dip after the pandemic, down to around 71% in 2023-24, but then it went back up. Grade 6 students had a slight increase (from around 81% to 85%).

We expected there to be a bigger change. From just looking at this graph, it looks like there has not been much change in reading across Ontario. However, this is an average across over 3,500 schools, so we wanted to know if all schools actually stayed the same or if some improved and some got worse. So we divided them into 5 groups (fifths) based on the percentage of children in the area who live in low-income households.

## How big is the gap between the richest and poorest schools, and is it closing?

```{r s2-data}
gap_df <- elem |>
  filter(income_group %in% c("Most affluent fifth", "Highest-poverty fifth")) |>
  group_by(year, income_group) |>
  summarise(`Grade 3` = mean(g3_read, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Grade 6` = mean(g6_read, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Grade 3`, `Grade 6`), names_to = "grade", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(year_short = year_label(as.integer(substr(year, 1, 4))))

gap_tbl <- gap_df |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = income_group, values_from = pct) |>
  mutate(gap = `Most affluent fifth` - `Highest-poverty fifth`)
```

```{r fig2, fig.height = 4.4}
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = gap_tbl,
               aes(y = year_short, yend = year_short,
                   x = `Highest-poverty fifth`, xend = `Most affluent fifth`),
               colour = "grey80", linewidth = 2.2) +
  geom_point(data = gap_df, aes(x = pct, y = year_short, colour = income_group),
             size = 3.2) +
  geom_text(data = gap_tbl,
            aes(x = `Most affluent fifth` + 1.2, y = year_short,
                label = paste0(round(gap), " pts")),
            hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = "grey25") +
  facet_wrap(~ grade) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = income_cols[c("Most affluent fifth", "Highest-poverty fifth")],
                      name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(58, 97), labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +

  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  labs(title = "Figure 2. The Grade 3 gap is stuck; the Grade 6 gap is narrowing",
       subtitle = "Share of students meeting the reading standard:\nmost affluent vs highest-poverty fifth of schools",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = source_note) +
  theme_story +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))
```

By dividing the schools into income groups we could see that the average was hiding a big difference. In Grade 3, the share of students meeting the standard in the most affluent fifth was around 15 to 16 percentage points higher than in the highest-poverty fifth (Figure 2). This did not change much from 2017-18 to 2024-25. This is a big difference, as in a class of 30 it means around 5 more children in a high-poverty school not meeting the provincial standard.

In Grade 6 we were surprised to see that the gap decreased. Before the pandemic the gap was around the same as Grade 3 (around 15 points). However, once testing resumed in 2021-22 the gap was around 11 points, and in 2024-25 it was around 10. So although the gap stayed the same in Grade 3, it was smaller in Grade 6. The Grade 3 class of 2021-22 is the Grade 6 class of 2024-25, so we decided to look at these students.

## Do students in poorer schools catch up from Grade 3 to Grade 6?

```{r s3-data}
g3_2021 <- elem |>
  filter(year == "2021-2022") |>
  select(school_number, income_group, g3 = g3_read)
g6_2024 <- elem |>
  filter(year == "2024-2025") |>
  select(school_number, g6 = g6_read)

follow <- inner_join(g3_2021, g6_2024, by = "school_number") |>
  filter(!is.na(g3), !is.na(g6))

follow_avg <- follow |>
  group_by(income_group) |>
  summarise(n_schools = n(), g3 = mean(g3), g6 = mean(g6)) |>
  mutate(gain = g6 - g3)
```

```{r fig3, fig.height = 4.6}
follow_long <- follow_avg |>
  pivot_longer(c(g3, g6), names_to = "when", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(when = if_else(when == "g3", "Grade 3\n(2021-22)", "Grade 6\n(2024-25)"))

labs_g3 <- follow_avg |>
  mutate(when = "Grade 3\n(2021-22)", y = g3 + c(0.6, -0.6, 0, 0, 0),
         txt = paste0(round(g3), "%"))
labs_g6 <- follow_avg |>
  mutate(when = "Grade 6\n(2024-25)", y = g6 + c(1.4, -0.2, 0.8, -0.4, 0),
         txt = paste0(round(g6), "%  ", income_group, " (+", round(gain), ")"))

ggplot(follow_long, aes(x = when, y = pct, group = income_group, colour = income_group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8) +
  geom_text(data = labs_g3, aes(y = y, label = txt), hjust = 1, nudge_x = -0.06,
            size = 3.3) +
  geom_text(data = labs_g6, aes(y = y, label = txt), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.06,
            size = 3.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = income_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.45, 1.75))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Figure 3. Students in high-poverty schools gain the most",
       subtitle = "Same schools, mostly the same students: Grade 3 reading and three years\nlater in Grade 6 (points gained in brackets)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = source_note) +
  theme_story +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

We compared the Grade 3 results in 2021-22 to the Grade 6 results 3 years later. All groups improved, however the high-poverty schools improved the most (around 16 points) compared to the most affluent schools (around 11 points) (Figure 3). This meant that by Grade 6 the gap between the two groups had decreased from around 15 points to around 10. We looked at the previous class (Grade 3 in 2018-19 to Grade 6 in 2021-22) and saw this trend again, however it was not as big (the gap went from about 14.5 points to 11.5).

Something to note is that the most affluent schools were already high, and by Grade 6 they were close to 90% (around 89%), so they did not have much room to improve. However, the high-poverty schools started so far behind that the gap did not fully close. The highest-poverty schools also have more students whose first language is not English. In 2017-18 it was about 36% of students on average, compared to 11% in the most affluent schools, so we wanted to see if this was the reason for the gap.

## Is the gap really about English learners?

```{r s4-data}
lang_year2 <- elem |>
  drop_na(first_lang_not_eng) |>
  mutate(lang_group = cut(first_lang_not_eng,
                          breaks = c(-Inf, 10, 30, Inf),
                          labels = c("10% or fewer", "10% to 30%", "More than 30%"))) |>
  group_by(start_year, lang_group) |>
  summarise(`Grade 3` = mean(g3_read, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Grade 6` = mean(g6_read, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_schools = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Grade 3`, `Grade 6`), names_to = "grade", values_to = "avg_read") |>
  mutate(period = if_else(start_year <= 2018, "before", "after"))
```


```{r fig4, fig.height = 4.6}
ggplot(lang_year2, aes(x = year_label(start_year), y = avg_read, colour = lang_group,
                       group = interaction(lang_group, period))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +

  geom_vline(xintercept = 2.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  facet_wrap(~ grade) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = lang_cols,
                      name = "Students whose first language isn't English:") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(65, 90), labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(title.position = "top")) +
  labs(title = "Figure 4. Reading results don't fall steadily as the share of\nmultilingual students rises",
       subtitle = "Average share of students meeting the reading standard\n(dashed line: no tests in 2019-20 and 2020-21)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = source_note) +
  theme_story +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8))
```

We also examined whether schools with different proportions of students whose first language is not English demonstrate differences in reading performance. Figure 4 compares the average share of students who attained the provincial reading standard across these groups for both Grade 3 and Grade 6. Contrary to our expectation, the findings did not align with our initial assumption. Before EQAO testing was cancelled in 2019-20 and 2020-21, schools where 10% or fewer of students’ first language is not English generally recorded slightly lower reading scores than those where this proportion is 30% or more. Yet, the differences between the two groups were relatively small. 

A more noticeable trend emerges among schools in the middle category. Those where students with a first language other than English account for 10% to 30% of total enrolment generally achieved the highest average results in almost every year, across both grades. Following the resumption of testing, schools with the lowest proportion of these students were seen to improve and their averages increased to levels comparable with the middle group in 2024-25. A similar improvement was not observed in Grade 6.


## Limitations

All the data we have is in percentages for the whole school. We have not weighted the data, so a school with 100 students counts the same as a school with 700 students. This means we cannot say anything about individual students. We have data for 3,525 regular English-language public and Catholic elementary schools.

There were also a few issues with the data. Schools where fewer than 10 students took the test do not have any data, which means that some small schools are missing. In Grade 3 there is no data for around 1 in 9 school-years. There are numbers for 2019-20 and 2020-21, but there were no EQAO tests in those years due to the pandemic. We checked this and found that 99.9% of the Grade 3 values were exactly the same as 2018-19, so we removed these years. In 2023-24 the numbers were in decimal format (e.g. 0.73), so we multiplied them by 100. The low-income numbers also change to new census data in 2022-23, which causes a big drop (from about 19% to 9% on average). Because of this, we put each school into the income group it was in during 2017-18.

When comparing Grade 3 and Grade 6, students move schools, so it is not exactly the same students. The most affluent schools also had little room to improve. The test was also online after the pandemic, so there may be some differences in the results. If we had student-level data or weighted the data by the number of students, we could be more precise with our findings.

## Conclusion
Ontario’s average reading results have remained relatively stable, yet the overall trend hides a persistent achievement gap between schools in different income areas. About 74% of Grade 3 students in the average school continue to meet the reading standard after seven years. However, schools in the highest-poverty group score approximately 16 percentage points lower than those in the most affluent, with little improvement over time. 

Nonetheless, our findings suggest that this gap can be reduced. By Grade 6, the difference in proportion of students meeting the provincial reading standard between the most affluent and highest-poverty schools had narrowed to about 10 percentage points (from about 15). As we followed the same cohorts of schools from Grade 3 to Grade 6, we discovered that schools in the highest-poverty group make the largest gains. Despite the improvement, the gap between the two groups remained significant. This suggests providing additional reading support at a younger age could be especially crucial.

In addition, language diversity does not appear to be a major factor to the disparity of reading achievements. Schools with a larger share of students whose first language is not English do not necessarily perform worse in reading. In fact, schools where these students made up 10% to 30% of total enrollment tend to perform the best. This suggests that socioeconomic factors may be more closely related to differences in reading achievements than the language background of students. 

One key takeaway is that disparities in reading performance are already significant by Grade 3. While high-poverty schools show greater progress by Grade 6, they still struggle to catch up with the most affluent schools. This raises an important question for policymakers and educators: should interventions begin even sooner to help bridge the gap, if these inequalities emerge so early?
